title: Full Speed Ahead: SpaceX Books a $40 Billion Passage Through the AI Iceberg Field
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

SpaceX enters $40 billion deal with Apollo for AI chip financing

SpaceX has secured a binding financing commitment for approximately $40 billion in GPUs and related equipment through an entity managed by Apollo Global Management. The arrangement will support NVIDIA Vera Rubin deployments for its terrestrial computing infrastructure, expanding capacity for Grok and cloud services customers. SpaceX describes it as the largest committed GPU financing to date.

Under the proposed structure, the Apollo-managed entity will purchase equipment and lease it to SpaceX in separate delivery tranches. Each lease will run approximately five to five-and-a-quarter years. Closing is expected before year-end 2026, subject to conditions, with equipment deliveries and lease commencement anticipated during the first half of 2027.

Apollo and Goldman Sachs lead the financing, with Goldman serving as sole structuring agent. BlackRock-managed funds, Goldman Sachs Asset Management and KKR-advised capital accounts have also made anchor commitments.

Why It Matters
The agreement illustrates how access to capital is becoming a competitive advantage in AI infrastructure. Advanced processors deliver value only when companies can finance, install and operate them at scale. This structure gives SpaceX another funding channel while spreading equipment payments across multiple years.

For the semiconductor industry, the commitment provides a substantial financing foundation for next-generation hardware deployment. Its potential effects extend beyond GPUs to the memory, networking, cooling and power infrastructure required to support productive computing clusters.

The economics still depend on execution. SpaceX must bring equipment online efficiently, sustain utilization and generate returns while newer processors continue entering the market. Leasing spreads payments over time but retains substantial financial obligations.

The approximately $40 billion figure represents expected principal payments; interest and certain expenses are additional. Ultimately, the transaction’s importance lies in connecting institutional capital with deployable computing capacity—turning ambitious AI expansion plans into a financed infrastructure program with a defined delivery timetable.
